title: Healthy snacks at the checkout counter: A lab and field study on the impact of shelf arrangement and assortment structure on consumer choices
abstract: BACKGROUND: The essence of nudging is to adapt the environment in which consumers make decisions to help them make better choices, without forcing certain outcomes upon them. To determine how consumers can effectively be guided to select healthier snacks, we examine the effect of manipulating the assortment structure and shelf layout of an impulse display including both healthy and unhealthy snacks near the checkout counter of a canteen. METHODS: Both a lab and field study applied a two-factor experimental design manipulating snack offerings both in an on-screen choice environment and a natural environment (hospital staff restaurant). Shelf arrangement (i.e. accessibility) was altered by putting healthy snacks at higher shelves versus lower shelves. Assortment structure (i.e. availability) was altered by offering an assortment that either included 25% or 75% healthy snacks. Participants in the lab study (n = 158) made a choice from a shelf display. A brief survey following snack selection asked participants to evaluate the assortment and their choice. The field experiment took place in a hospital canteen. Daily sales data were collected for a period of four weeks. On completion of the field study, employees (n = 92) filled out a questionnaire about all four displays and rated their attractiveness, healthiness and perceived freedom of choice. RESULTS: The lab study showed a higher probability of healthy snack choice when 75% of the assortment consisted of healthy snacks compared to conditions with 25% healthy snack assortments, even though choices were not rated less satisfying or more restrictive. Regarding shelf display location of healthy snacks, no significant differences were observed. There was also no significant shelf arrangement by assortment structure interactive effect. The field study replicated these findings, in that this assortment structure led to higher sales of healthy snacks. Sales of unhealthy and total snacks were not impacted by manipulations (no main or interaction effects). Employees preferred shelf displays including a larger healthy snack assortment located at top shelves. Employees also felt more freedom in choice when healthy snacks were displayed at top shelves compared to lower shelves. CONCLUSIONS: Overall, results suggest that increasing the prominence of healthy snacks by enlarging their availability, while permitting access to unhealthy snacks, is a promising strategy to promote sales. These results point to the importance of nudging strategies to encourage healthier snack patterns.

claims.text: In the lab experiment, participants exposed to a shelf with 75% healthy snacks were 2.9 times more likely to select a healthy snack than those exposed to a shelf with 25% healthy snacks.
In the lab study, shelf display location (top versus bottom) had no significant effect on healthy snack choice.
In the lab study, there was no significant interaction effect between shelf arrangement and assortment structure on healthy snack choice.
In the lab study, participants in the 75% healthy snack condition rated the assortment as significantly less realistic than those in the 25% healthy snack condition.
In the field study, an assortment of 75% healthy snacks significantly increased daily sales of healthy snacks compared to an assortment of 25% healthy snacks.
In the field study, snack display manipulations had no significant main or interactive effects on the sales of unhealthy snacks or total snacks.
In the hospital employee survey, shelf displays with 75% healthy snacks and healthy snacks on top shelves were rated as significantly more attractive and healthier.
In the hospital employee survey, displaying healthy snacks on top shelves significantly increased perceived freedom in product choice compared to displaying them on lower shelves.

limitations.text: The experimental design did not allow for disentangling the combined effect of the number of options and variety of options within snack categories.
The choice task in the lab study had an artificial nature and relied exclusively on student participants.
The total number of snacks sold during the four-week field study was relatively small (291 snacks).
Fresh fruit was priced lower (0.50 euro) than other snacks (0.85 euro) in the field study, potentially confounding the availability effect.
It is unclear whether the intervention produces sustained changes in snack choices or if healthy snack choices are compensated for later in the day.
Previous experimental studies exploring food accessibility provide inconclusive results due to disparate manipulations and settings.

future_work.text: Disentangle the combined effect of the number of options versus variety of options within healthy and unhealthy snack categories.
Identify other factors that gently nudge consumers toward healthier snack choices and test their effectiveness across various contexts beyond canteens.

methodologies.name: Lab-based online simulated choice experiment
methodologies.description: A 2x2 between-subject experimental design where participants made a hypothetical snack selection from a virtual 16-item display varying shelf arrangement and assortment proportion.
conditions: Shelf arrangement: healthy snacks on top shelves vs. bottom shelves

methodologies.name: Hospital canteen field experiment and post-intervention survey
methodologies.description: A 4-week field intervention manipulating physical shelf displays at a hospital checkout counter with daily sales monitoring, followed by an employee evaluation survey (n = 92).
